title: Write a Script with Options: getopts and while read
intro: The earlier bash labs hardcoded their inputs. A script other people run needs options (-f, -t, -v), a usage message, and sensible errors for bad input. It also needs to read a file line by line correctly, which most hand-written scripts get wrong. Write a script that checks every host listed in a file.

steps.prompt:
Write check-hosts.sh:
(1) 'set -euo pipefail'.
(2) A function usage() that prints 'Usage: $0 -f hosts_file [-t timeout] [-v]' to stderr and runs 'exit 2'.
(3) Defaults: file="", timeout=5, verbose=0.
(4) Parse options with: while getopts ":f:t:vh" opt; do case "$opt" in ... esac; done
    f) sets file="$OPTARG"; t) sets timeout="$OPTARG"; v) sets verbose=1; h) calls usage;
    \?) prints 'Unknown option: -$OPTARG' to stderr and calls usage;
    :) prints 'Option -$OPTARG needs a value' to stderr and calls usage.
(5) After the loop: shift $((OPTIND - 1))
(6) If file is empty, call usage: [[ -n "$file" ]] || usage
(7) Read the file line by line with: while IFS= read -r host; do ... done < "$file"
    Skip blank lines and lines starting with #. For each host run
    ping -c 1 -W "$timeout" "$host" (output to /dev/null). If it fails, print 'DOWN <host>' to stderr.
    If it succeeds and verbose is 1, print 'UP <host>'.
steps.hint:
The option loop:
  while getopts ":f:t:vh" opt; do
    case "$opt" in
      f) file="$OPTARG" ;;
      ...
      \?) echo "Unknown option: -$OPTARG" >&2; usage ;;
      :) echo "Option -$OPTARG needs a value" >&2; usage ;;
    esac
  done
The skip line inside the read loop: [[ -z "$host" || "$host" == \#* ]] && continue
The file is fed to the loop at the end: done < "$file" (not 'cat file | while', and not 'for host in $(cat file)').
steps.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Check every host listed in a file.
# Usage: check-hosts.sh -f hosts_file [-t timeout] [-v]
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
  echo "Usage: $0 -f hosts_file [-t timeout] [-v]" >&2
  exit 2
}

file=""
timeout=5
verbose=0

while getopts ":f:t:vh" opt; do
  case "$opt" in
    f) file="$OPTARG" ;;
    t) timeout="$OPTARG" ;;
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    h) usage ;;
    \?) echo "Unknown option: -$OPTARG" >&2; usage ;;
    :) echo "Option -$OPTARG needs a value" >&2; usage ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))

[[ -n "$file" ]] || usage

while IFS= read -r host; do
  [[ -z "$host" || "$host" == \#* ]] && continue
  if ping -c 1 -W "$timeout" "$host" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    if [[ "$verbose" -eq 1 ]]; then
      echo "UP   $host"
    fi
  else
    echo "DOWN $host" >&2
  fi
done < "$file"
steps.fake_output:
$ ./check-hosts.sh -v -t 2 -f hosts.txt
UP   web-1.internal
DOWN db-2.internal
UP   cache-1.internal
$ ./check-hosts.sh -t
Option -t needs a value
Usage: ./check-hosts.sh -f hosts_file [-t timeout] [-v]
$ echo $?
2
steps.explanation: The script takes options in any order, explains itself when misused, and reads the host file one line at a time without mangling it.
steps.why: The details each prevent a specific bug. (1) In the getopts string, a letter followed by a colon takes a value (f: and t:), and the leading colon turns on silent mode, so you handle errors yourself: '?' for an unknown option and ':' for a missing value, each with OPTARG holding the offending letter. (2) 'shift $((OPTIND - 1))' removes the parsed options, leaving any positional arguments in "$@". (3) Exit code 2 is the convention for 'you called me wrong', distinct from 1 for 'I ran and failed'. (4) 'while IFS= read -r' is the only correct way to read lines: IFS= keeps leading and trailing spaces, and -r stops backslashes being eaten. 'for host in $(cat file)' splits on every space and expands wildcards. (5) 'cat file | while' runs the loop in a subshell, so variables set inside it (a failure counter, say) are lost when it ends; 'done < file' keeps the loop in the current shell. (6) One trap this script avoids by using ping: a command inside the loop that reads standard input, ssh above all, swallows the rest of the file and the loop ends after one host. Give such commands '< /dev/null', or use 'ssh -n'. getopts handles only short options; for --long options, scripts loop over "$@" with a case statement instead.
